THOUGHT: The patient has a long-standing, asymptomatic, linear/arc-shaped depressed groove on the forehead/scalp with scarring alopecia. Key histologic findings are a lymphocytic perifollicular/periappendageal infiltrate and a lobular panniculitis with hyaline fat necrosis in the subcutis. Direct immunofluorescence shows granular deposition of multiple immunoreactants (IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, fibrinogen) in dermal vessels. ANA and anti-dsDNA are negative and there are no systemic lupus symptoms. Clinically the depressed linear forehead/scalp lesion resembles en coup de sabre (linear scleroderma), but the histology (lobular lymphocytic panniculitis with hyaline fat necrosis) and positive granular DIF are classic for lupus panniculitis (lupus profundus), including its linear variant that can mimic en coup de sabre and cause scarring alopecia. DLE (discoid lupus) and lichen planopilaris can produce scarring alopecia and have lymphocytic follicular infiltrates, but they lack the prominent lobular panniculitis with hyaline fat necrosis and the same DIF pattern is more supportive of lupus. Localized steroid-induced lipoatrophy could produce a depressed groove after injections but would not show lobular panniculitis with hyaline necrosis or the multispecific granular DIF. Therefore the most likely diagnosis is lupus panniculitis (lupus profundus), linear variant, with other considerations listed below.

DIAGNOSIS:
1) Lupus panniculitis (lupus profundus), linear variant (mimicking en coup de sabre)
2) Linear morphea (en coup de sabre, localized scleroderma)
3) Discoid lupus erythematosus with underlying panniculitis/atrophy
4) Lichen planopilaris (linear/cicatricial alopecia variant)
5) Localized corticosteroid-induced lipoatrophy (post-injection)

Case Information:
A man in his 50s presented with an asymptomatic, arc-shaped, depressed skin groove on the left side of his forehead, frontal scalp, and vertex area. Localized linear hair loss and hair thinning on the left scalp area were observed. The patient reported that when the lesion had begun approximately 10 years earlier, he had received 2 doses of intralesional steroid via injection on a small bald patch on the vertex. Thereafter, the lesion gradually progressed to the frontal scalp and eventually made a linear furrow on the left side of his forehead. The patient denied any trauma history and had no history of connective tissue disease nor any evidence of systemic involvement, such as arthralgia, photosensitivity, or skin rashes.

Physical Examination:
Examination revealed 2 long, curved-line, depressed, alopecic patches on the left side of the vertex and frontal scalp area extending to the left eyebrow. The lesions measured (length × width) 7 × 2 cm and 6 × 1 cm, respectively. Dermoscopic examination of the alopecic area revealed several short vellus hairs, yellow dots, and honeycomb hyperpigmentation; however, broken hairs were not seen. The result of a hair pull test was negative.
